Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Consider the family S of irreducible plane curves of degree n with d nodes and k cusps as singularities. Let W be an irreducible component of S. We consider the natural rational map from W to the moduli space of curves of genus g=(n-1)(n-2)/2-d-k. We define the "number of moduli of W" as the dimension of the image of W with respect to this map. If W has the expected dimension equal to 3n+g-1-k, then the number of moduli of W is at most equal to the min(3g-3, 3g-3+\rho-k), dove \rho is the Brill-Neother number of the linear series of degree n and dimension 2 on a smooth curve of genus g. We say that W has the expected number of moduli if the equality holds. In this paper we construct examples of families of irreducible plane curves with nodes and cusps as singularities having expected number of moduli and with non-positive Brill-Noether number.

Consider the family \(S\) of irreducible plane curves of degree \(n\) whose singularities consist of \(d\) nodes and \(k\) cusps. Let \(W\) be an irreducible component of \(S\). We consider the natural rational map from \(W\) to the moduli space of curves of genus
\[
g=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}-d-k.
\]
We define the “number of moduli of \(W\)” as the dimension of the image of \(W\) under this map.

If \(W\) has the expected dimension, namely \(3n+g-1-k\), then the number of moduli of \(W\) is at most
\[
\min(3g-3,\; 3g-3+\rho-k),
\]
where \(\rho\) is the Brill–Noether number of the linear series of degree \(n\) and dimension \(2\) on a smooth curve of genus \(g\). We say that \(W\) has the expected number of moduli if equality holds.

In this paper, we construct examples of families of irreducible plane curves with nodes and cusps as singularities that have the expected number of moduli and non-positive Brill–Noether number.

The text investigates families of irreducible plane algebraic curves of degree \(n\) whose only singularities are \(d\) nodes and \(k\) cusps. Such curves form a parameter space, often denoted by a suitable equisingular family, whose points correspond to plane curves with precisely these prescribed singularities.

For a curve of degree \(n\) with \(d\) nodes and \(k\) cusps, the geometric genus is

\[
g=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}-d-k.
\]

This is obtained from the arithmetic genus of a smooth plane curve of degree \(n\), namely \(\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}\), by subtracting the contributions of the nodes and cusps, each of which lowers the genus by one.

Let \(W\) be an irreducible component of the family of such curves. To a general curve in \(W\), one can associate its normalization, which is a smooth curve of genus \(g\). This gives a natural rational map from \(W\) to the moduli space \(\mathcal M_g\) of smooth curves of genus \(g\):

\[
W \dashrightarrow \mathcal M_g.
\]

The number of moduli of \(W\) is defined to be the dimension of the image of this map. In other words, it measures how many parameters are needed to describe the isomorphism classes of the smooth curves obtained by normalizing the plane curves in the family \(W\).

A central issue is to compare the dimension of \(W\) with the dimension of its image in \(\mathcal M_g\). If \(W\) has the expected dimension, namely

\[
\dim W = 3n+g-1-k,
\]

then the number of moduli of \(W\) is bounded above by

\[
\min(3g-3,\; 3g-3+\rho-k),
\]

where

\[
\rho = 3n - 2g - 6
\]

is the relevant Brill-Noether number for plane curves of degree \(n\). The first term, \(3g-3\), is the dimension of the full moduli space \(\mathcal M_g\) for \(g \geq 2\). The second term reflects the additional restrictions imposed by the existence of a plane model of degree \(n\) with \(k\) cusps. Thus, when \(\rho-k\) is negative, the family cannot dominate the entire moduli space; its image must have smaller dimension.

The paper is concerned not only with establishing these general bounds, but also with showing that they are sharp in significant cases. In particular, it constructs explicit examples of irreducible components \(W\) of families of plane curves with nodes and cusps that have the expected dimension and also attain the expected number of moduli. These examples are especially notable because they occur in cases where the Brill-Noether number \(\rho\) is non-positive. In such situations, the corresponding curves are special from the Brill-Noether point of view, and the construction demonstrates that even under these restrictive conditions, the predicted dimension and moduli behavior can still be achieved.

The paper investigates families of irreducible plane curves of degree \(n\) having precisely \(d\) nodes and \(k\) cusps as singularities. Such curves have geometric genus

\[
g=\binom{n-1}{2}-d-k,
\]

and their normalizations determine smooth curves of genus \(g\). This gives a natural rational map from each irreducible component of the corresponding equisingular parameter space of plane curves to the moduli space \(\mathcal M_g\) of smooth curves of genus \(g\). A central question is to understand the dimension of the image of this map, or equivalently, how many moduli the family of normalized curves carries.

In general, one expects the dimension of the image in \(\mathcal M_g\) to be governed by the dimension of the family of plane curves, after factoring out projective equivalence. When this expectation is satisfied, the component is said to have the expected number of moduli. Classical Brill–Noether theory predicts the existence and dimension of linear series on a general curve, and the relevant Brill–Noether number in this setting measures the expected behavior of the \(g^2_n\) giving the plane model. When this number is positive, the expected moduli behavior is more naturally anticipated. The subtle case occurs when the Brill–Noether number is zero or negative, since then a general curve of genus \(g\) should not carry such a plane linear series, and one might expect the corresponding families to have fewer moduli than predicted.

The main contribution of the paper is to show that this pessimistic expectation is not always justified. The authors construct explicit families of irreducible plane curves with prescribed numbers of nodes and cusps whose associated components in the equisingular parameter space still have the expected number of moduli, even though the relevant Brill–Noether number is non-positive. These examples demonstrate that the expected moduli behavior can persist outside the range where Brill–Noether theory would most directly suggest it.

Thus, the paper broadens the known scope of equisingular families of plane curves with well-behaved moduli maps. It shows that components of Severi-type varieties with nodes and cusps may exhibit the expected dimension of their image in \(\mathcal M_g\) even in Brill–Noether-special situations. In particular, the results provide evidence that the relationship between plane models of curves, singularity conditions, and moduli is richer than what is predicted solely by the sign of the Brill–Noether number.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a paper about families of irreducible plane curves of degree n with d nodes and k cusps, their expected dimension, moduli map, and examples with expected number of moduli when the Brill-Noether number is non-positive.
counterfactuals.output:
We study families \(V_{n,d,k}\) of irreducible plane curves of degree \(n\) with precisely \(d\) nodes and \(k\) ordinary cusps as singularities. For such a curve the geometric genus is  
\[
g=\binom{n-1}{2}-d-k,
\]
and the expected dimension of the corresponding equisingular family is  
\[
\dim V_{n,d,k}^{\mathrm{exp}}
=\frac{n(n+3)}2-d-2k
=3n+g-1-k.
\]
We analyze the natural moduli map
\[
\Pi_{\Sigma}: V_{n,d,k}\dashrightarrow \mathcal M_g,
\]
which sends a plane curve to the isomorphism class of its normalization, and compare the dimension of its image with the expected number of moduli. In particular, after quotienting by projective automorphisms of the plane, the expected dimension of the image is
\[
\dim \Pi_{\Sigma}(V_{n,d,k})_{\mathrm{exp}}
=
3n+g-9-k
=
3g-3+\rho-k,
\]
where
\[
\rho=\rho(2,g,n)=3n-2g-6
\]
is the Brill–Noether number associated with \(g^2_n\)’s on curves of genus \(g\).

Special attention is given to the case \(\rho\le 0\), where a general curve of genus \(g\) is not expected to carry a plane model of degree \(n\). In this range, the expected number of moduli of a component of \(V_{n,d,k}\) is \(3g-3+\rho-k\), provided this number is non-negative. We present examples of families of nodal-cuspidal plane curves whose components have the expected dimension and whose moduli maps have image of the expected dimension, thereby giving families with the expected number of moduli in the Brill–Noether non-positive range. These examples illustrate how the presence of cusps decreases the number of moduli and provide evidence for the expected behavior of Severi–Enriques varieties with prescribed nodes and cusps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main idea of a research article on Severi varieties of plane curves with nodes and cusps, defining the number of moduli of an irreducible component and stating the expected moduli result involving the Brill-Noether number.
counterfactuals.output:
The article studies **Severi varieties of plane curves** of degree \(n\) having prescribed singularities, specifically **\(d\) nodes** and **\(k\) cusps**. Such a curve has geometric genus

\[
g=\binom{n-1}{2}-d-k.
\]

The main question is: **how many moduli do the normalizations of curves in an irreducible component of such a Severi variety carry?** In other words, when one varies a plane curve with fixed degree and fixed numbers of nodes and cusps, how large is the resulting family of smooth curves in the moduli space \(\mathcal M_g\)?

Given an irreducible component \(\Sigma\) of the Severi variety, there is a natural rational map

\[
\Pi_\Sigma : \Sigma \dashrightarrow \mathcal M_g
\]

sending a singular plane curve to the isomorphism class of its normalization. The **number of moduli of \(\Sigma\)** is defined as

\[
\dim \Pi_\Sigma(\Sigma),
\]

the dimension of its image in \(\mathcal M_g\).

The expected dimension of the equisingular family is

\[
\dim \Sigma = 3n+g-1-k,
\]

because nodes impose one condition and cusps impose two. Since plane curves related by projective transformations of \(\mathbb P^2\) have the same abstract normalization, one subtracts the dimension \(8\) of \(\operatorname{PGL}(3)\). Thus the expected number of moduli is

\[
\dim \Sigma -8 = 3n+g-9-k.
\]

This can be rewritten using the Brill–Noether number for plane linear series,

\[
\rho(2,g,n)=3n-2g-6.
\]

Then

\[
3n+g-9-k
=
3g-3+\rho(2,g,n)-k.
\]

Since the image cannot have dimension larger than \(\dim \mathcal M_g=3g-3\), the expected moduli statement is that an irreducible component \(\Sigma\) should have

\[
\dim \Pi_\Sigma(\Sigma)
=
\min\left\{3g-3,\; 3g-3+\rho(2,g,n)-k\right\}.
\]

Thus the article investigates when components of Severi varieties of nodal-cuspidal plane curves have this **expected number of moduli**, governed by the Brill–Noether number and the number of cusps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain in mathematical language the setting where W is an irreducible component of the family of plane curves of degree n with d nodes and k cusps, genus g, expected dimension 3n+g-1-k, and expected number of moduli.
counterfactuals.output:
Let  

\[
\mathbb P^N=\mathbb P\bigl(H^0(\mathbb P^2,\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(n))\bigr),
\qquad 
N=\binom{n+2}{2}-1=\frac{n(n+3)}2,
\]

be the projective space parametrizing plane curves of degree \(n\). Consider the locally closed equisingular locus

\[
\Sigma_{d,k}^{n}\subset \mathbb P^N
\]

whose general point corresponds to an irreducible plane curve

\[
\Gamma\subset \mathbb P^2
\]

of degree \(n\) having exactly \(d\) nodes and \(k\) ordinary cusps as its only singularities.

If \(\nu:C\to \Gamma\) is the normalization, then the geometric genus of \(\Gamma\) is

\[
g=p_g(C)=p_a(\Gamma)-d-k
=\binom{n-1}{2}-d-k.
\]

Let

\[
W\subset \Sigma_{d,k}^{n}
\]

be an irreducible component. Since a node imposes one condition and a cusp imposes two conditions on plane curves, the expected dimension of \(W\) is

\[
\dim_{\mathrm{exp}} W
=
N-d-2k.
\]

Using

\[
g=\binom{n-1}{2}-d-k,
\]

one rewrites this as

\[
\dim_{\mathrm{exp}} W
=
3n+g-1-k.
\]

Thus \(W\) is said to have the expected dimension if

\[
\dim W=3n+g-1-k.
\]

There is a natural moduli map

\[
\Pi:W\dashrightarrow \mathcal M_g,
\qquad 
[\Gamma]\longmapsto [C],
\]

sending a plane curve to the isomorphism class of its normalization. The “number of moduli” of \(W\) means

\[
\dim \Pi(W)\subseteq \mathcal M_g.
\]

Since plane curves are considered up to projective equivalence, the fibers of \(\Pi\) are expected to contain the orbits of \(\operatorname{PGL}_3\), of dimension \(8\). Therefore the expected dimension of the moduli image is

\[
\dim_{\mathrm{exp}}\Pi(W)
=
\min\{\,3g-3,\ \dim_{\mathrm{exp}}W-8\,\}.
\]

For \(g\ge 2\), this becomes

\[
\dim_{\mathrm{exp}}\Pi(W)
=
\min\{\,3g-3,\ 3n+g-9-k\,\}.
\]

Equivalently, using the Brill–Noether number for \(g^2_n\)’s,

\[
\rho(2,g,n)=3n-2g-6,
\]

one may write

\[
3n+g-9-k
=
3g-3+\rho(2,g,n)-k.
\]

Hence \(W\) is said to have the expected number of moduli if

\[
\dim \Pi(W)
=
\min\{\,3g-3,\ 3g-3+\rho(2,g,n)-k\,\}.
\]

In summary, the setting is an irreducible component \(W\) of the equisingular family of irreducible degree-\(n\) plane curves with \(d\) nodes and \(k\) cusps, whose normalization has genus

\[
g=\binom{n-1}{2}-d-k,
\]

whose expected dimension is

\[
3n+g-1-k,
\]

and whose expected number of moduli is the expected dimension of its image in \(\mathcal M_g\), namely

\[
\min\{3g-3,\ 3n+g-9-k\}.
\]

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise introduction/abstract for a paper constructing examples of nodal-cuspidal plane curve families with expected number of moduli and non-positive Brill-Noether number.
counterfactuals.output:
We construct new families of irreducible plane curves with prescribed nodes and cusps whose normalizations have non-positive Brill–Noether number, yet whose moduli vary in the expected dimension. More precisely, for suitable triples \((d,n,k)\), we exhibit components of the equiclassical/Severi variety of degree \(d\) plane curves with \(n\) nodes and \(k\) cusps such that the associated moduli map to \(\mathcal M_g\), where  
\[
g=\binom{d-1}{2}-n-k,
\]
has image of the expected dimension. These examples lie in the Brill–Noether special range, where the existence of a plane model imposes nontrivial constraints on the normalization, and therefore provide explicit evidence that expected-moduli behavior persists beyond the Brill–Noether positive regime. The construction combines deformation-theoretic criteria for nodal-cuspidal curves with explicit degenerations, yielding infinite series of components with controlled singularities and moduli.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
